```{r setup, include=FALSE}
site <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = site,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
```

`suest()` combines two or more separately fitted models so you can test
whether predictions, marginal effects, or other quantities differ across the
models. It supplies the joint robust covariance matrix those tests need, and
leaves calculating and presenting the quantities themselves to
[`marginaleffects`](https://marginaleffects.com/).

## Functions at a glance

- `suest()` combines two or more fitted models and calculates their joint
  covariance matrix. Its `twopart` option combines the two parts of
  [two-part models](two-part.html).
- `suest_newdata()` stacks the models' estimation samples, one block of rows
  per model.
- `suest_mi()` pools `suest()` results across multiply imputed datasets.
- The usual `marginaleffects` functions, including `predictions()`,
  `avg_comparisons()`, `avg_slopes()`, `hypotheses()`, and the plotting
  functions, work with the combined object, and `modelsummary()` makes
  tables from it.

## Installation and setup

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_github("tdmize/suest")
```

```{r libraries}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)
```

## Basic workflow

Two logit models of union membership, the second adding wages and work
experience:

```{r basic-workflow}
nlsw <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/nlsw88.dta"))
nlsw <- nlsw[!is.na(nlsw$union), ]
nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")] <- lapply(nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")], factor)

base <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south, family = binomial("logit"),
            data = nlsw)
adjusted <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south + wage + ttl_exp,
                family = binomial("logit"), data = nlsw)
combined <- suest(base, adjusted, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"))
combined
summary(combined)

effects <- avg_comparisons(combined, variables = "collgrad", newdata = nlsw)
effects
hypotheses(effects, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

The last command tests the difference between the two effects directly. That
is different from checking whether one effect is statistically significant and
the other is not.

## Tests on coefficients

`hypotheses()` lists the coefficients of every model with their joint robust
standard errors. `b1`, `b2`, ... refer to them in that order, so they can be
tested against each other across models:

```{r coefficients}
hypotheses(combined)
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "b2 = b6")
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "(b2 - b6) / b2 = 0")
```

## Supported models

### Single-level models

| Model | Fitted with |
|---|---|
| Linear regression | `lm()` |
| Binary logit, probit, and complementary log-log | `glm()`, `glm2::glm2()` |
| Ordered logit and probit | `MASS::polr()`, `ordinal::clm()` |
| Multinomial logit | `nnet::multinom()` |
| Poisson regression | `glm()`, `glm2::glm2()` |
| Negative binomial regression | `MASS::glm.nb()` |
| Constant-dispersion negative binomial (Stata's `nbreg, dispersion(constant)`) | `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` with `family = nbinom1()` |
| Zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial | `pscl::zeroinfl()` |
| Other GLMs with identity, log, logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log links | `glm()`, `glm2::glm2()` |
| Tobit regression | `censReg::censReg()`; predictions are the latent mean |
| Interval, censored, and parametric survival regression | `survival::survreg()` with a common scale |
| Gompertz and generalized gamma survival | `flexsurv::flexsurvreg()` with `dist = "gompertz"` or `"gengamma"` |
| Truncated regression | `truncreg::truncreg()` |
| Fractional response | `glm()` with `quasibinomial()`: logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log link |
| Beta regression | `betareg::betareg()` with a logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log link |
| Heteroskedastic probit and logit | `Rchoice::hetprob()` |
| Bivariate probit | `GJRM::gjrm()`, with the same or different predictors in each equation; `mvProbit::mvProbit()` with the same predictors |
| Instrumental-variable regression (two-stage least squares) | `fixest::feols()`, unweighted and without absorbed fixed effects |
| Instrumental-variable probit | `Rchoice::ivpml()`; predictions are average structural probabilities |
| Generalized ordered logit (gologit2), including partial proportional odds, with logit, probit, cloglog, log-log, or cauchit links | `VGAM::vglm()` with `cumulative(reverse = TRUE)`; for log-log, see [Notes on specific models](model-notes.html#generalized-ordered-models) |
| Heckman selection (maximum likelihood) | `sampleSelection::selection(method = "ml")` |

### Panel models

| Model | Fitted with |
|---|---|
| Linear fixed-, between-, and random-effects | `plm::plm()` with individual effects |
| Random-effects logit and probit | `pglm::pglm(model = "random", effect = "individual")` |
| Random-effects Poisson | `pglm::pglm(model = "random", effect = "individual", other = "sd")` |
| Fixed-effects Poisson | `fixest::fepois(y ~ x | id)` |
| Population-averaged (GEE) linear, logit, probit, complementary log-log, and Poisson | `geepack::geeglm()` with independence, exchangeable, ar1, or unstructured correlation |

### Multilevel models

| Model | Fitted with |
|---|---|
| Linear, random intercept | `nlme::lme(method = "ML")` |
| Linear (maximum likelihood) | `lme4::lmer(REML = FALSE)` |
| Logit, probit, complementary log-log, and Poisson | `lme4::glmer()`; with only a random intercept, any `nAGQ` |
| Logit, probit, complementary log-log, Poisson, negative binomial (mean or constant dispersion), linear, and Gamma (log link) | `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` |
| Ordered logit and probit | `ordinal::clmm()` |

Except for `nlme::lme()`, these models can have random slopes, several of
them, and a level nested in the grouping variable (three-level models); see
[Notes on specific models](model-notes.html#several-random-slopes-and-three-level-models).

### Survey models

| Model | Fitted with |
|---|---|
| Linear regression | `survey::svyglm()` |
| Binary logit, probit, and cloglog | `survey::svyglm()` with `quasibinomial()` |
| Poisson | `survey::svyglm()` with `quasipoisson()` |
| Ordered logit and probit | `survey::svyolr()` |
| Multinomial logit | `svyVGAM::svy_vglm()` with `multinomial()` |
| Negative binomial regression | `svyVGAM::svy_vglm()` with `negbinomial()` |
| Generalized ordered logit (gologit2), including partial proportional odds | `svyVGAM::svy_vglm()` with `cumulative(reverse = TRUE)` |
| Tobit, interval, and parametric survival regression | `survey::svysurvreg()` with a common scale |
| Instrumental-variable regression (two-stage least squares) | `survey::svyivreg()` |

See [Survey data](#survey-data) below.

### Combining models

Models can use the same, partially overlapping, or completely different
samples. Any single-level models can be combined, including models for
different outcomes and models for categorical outcomes. Results on different
scales are labeled separately rather than treated as directly comparable.

Random-effects models (`nlme::lme()`, `pglm()`, `glmmTMB()`, lme4, `clmm()`)
can be combined with each other, including different families, and with
linear, logit, probit, complementary log-log, Poisson, negative binomial, and
ordered logit and probit models, such as a logit model with a random-intercept
logit model. They must be unweighted and share one grouping variable (for
three-level models, the top level), and the system is clustered on that
variable. Other panel models (`plm()`, `geeglm()`) can be combined only with
models of the same kind.

Offsets work in most models, written in the formula or given in the `offset`
argument. They are not supported in `glmmTMB()`, lme4, `clmm()`, `pglm()`,
`fixest::fepois()`, `VGAM::vglm()`, `flexsurv::flexsurvreg()`, and
`GJRM::gjrm()` models. Survey models need them in the formula, as `offset()`.

A few models have settings worth knowing about; see
[Notes on specific models](model-notes.html).

## Different samples or groups

When the models are fitted to different samples, such as separate groups,
each model's effects are averaged over its own sample. That is the default
when `newdata` is left out; `newdata = suest_newdata(fit)` says the same thing
explicitly:

```{r groups}
south_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                   data = nlsw, subset = south == 1)
nonsouth_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                      data = nlsw, subset = south == 0)
fit_groups <- suest(south_model, nonsouth_model,
                    model_names = c("South", "Non-South"))

effects_groups <- avg_comparisons(fit_groups, variables = "collgrad",
                                  newdata = suest_newdata(fit_groups))
effects_groups
hypotheses(effects_groups, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

## Cluster-robust standard errors

Supply a cluster variable to get cluster-robust standard errors for the
combined models. The National Longitudinal Survey of Young Women follows the
same women over many years, so the same two models of union membership,
fitted to all the years, cluster on each woman's ID:

```{r cluster-example}
nlswork <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/nlswork.dta"))

base_p <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south, family = binomial("logit"),
              data = nlswork)
adjusted_p <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south + ln_wage + ttl_exp,
                  family = binomial("logit"), data = nlswork)
fit_clustered <- suest(base_p, adjusted_p, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
                       cluster = "idcode")

effects_clustered <- avg_comparisons(fit_clustered, variables = "collgrad")
effects_clustered
hypotheses(effects_clustered, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

`cluster` takes one or more column names, or a list with one vector, matrix,
or data frame matched to each model's estimation sample. An observation that
appears in more than one model must have the same cluster ID in each.
Observations in completely different samples can belong to the same cluster,
in which case the covariance between models can be nonzero.

Panel models cluster on the panel identifier by default. A cluster you supply
must contain whole panels.

## Probability weights

`suest` supports probability weights for linear, binary (logit, probit,
complementary log-log), fractional, Poisson, negative binomial, ordered logit
and probit, and multinomial logit models, and for other GLMs such as Gamma and
quasi-Poisson models. Fit each model with `weights =`, and tell `suest()` that
they are probability weights with `weight_type = "pweight"`. `wts = TRUE`
averages with the weights:

```{r pweight-example}
set.seed(376)
weighted <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500), z = rnorm(500))
weighted$mediator <- 0.5 * weighted$x - 0.3 * weighted$z + rnorm(500)
weighted$pw <- exp(0.2 * weighted$z + 0.1 * rnorm(500))
weighted$y <- 1 + 0.7 * weighted$x - 0.4 * weighted$z +
  0.6 * weighted$mediator + rnorm(500)

base_w <- lm(y ~ x + z, weights = pw, data = weighted)
adjusted_w <- lm(y ~ x + z + mediator, weights = pw, data = weighted)
fit_w <- suest(base_w, adjusted_w, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
               weight_type = "pweight")
fit_w

effects_w <- avg_comparisons(fit_w, variables = "x", wts = TRUE)
effects_w
hypotheses(effects_w, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

Weights must be positive and finite. An observation that appears in more than
one model must have the same weight in each; weights can differ for
observations in only one model, including completely different samples. When
the models have different samples, `wts = TRUE` averages each model over its
own sample with its own weights.

## Survey data

`suest` supports the survey models in the table above, fitted from one common
one-stage survey design, in any combination. Give `suest()` the design and a
variable that identifies each observation. The example uses the stratified
sample of California schools that comes with the `survey` package: does the
effect of the percentage of English language learners on a school's academic
performance index shrink once the percentage of students eligible for free
meals is held constant?

```{r survey-example}
library(survey)
data(api)
design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, fpc = ~fpc,
                    data = apistrat)
base_s <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell, design)
adjusted_s <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals, design)
fit_survey <- suest(base_s, adjusted_s, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
                    survey_design = design, observation_id = "snum")

effects_survey <- avg_slopes(fit_survey, variables = "ell", wts = TRUE)
effects_survey
hypotheses(effects_survey, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

If a model uses a subset (domain) of the data, fit it to `subset(design, ...)`
and still give `suest()` the full design. The joint covariance accounts for
strata, primary sampling units, and one-stage finite population corrections.
Replicate weights, multistage designs, calibration, and
probability-proportional-to-size designs are not supported.

## Multiple imputation

To combine results across imputed datasets, fit the same `suest` system in
each one. With `mice`, `with()` does this, and `marginaleffects` functions
then estimate within each imputation and pool the results with Rubin's
rules, including cross-model differences. The example imputes missing wages,
education, and occupation in an extract of the National Longitudinal Study of
Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), then asks whether the effect of
education on wages is smaller once part-time work and occupation are held
constant:

```{r mi-example}
ah <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4_mcar.dta"))
ah <- ah[c("wages", "edyrs", "woman", "age", "parttime", "occcat")]
ah$occcat <- factor(ah$occcat)
imp <- mice::mice(ah, m = 10, seed = 2307, printFlag = FALSE)

analyses <- with(imp, suest(
  lm(wages ~ edyrs + woman + age),
  lm(wages ~ edyrs + woman + age + parttime + occcat),
  model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted")
))
avg_comparisons(analyses, variables = "edyrs")
avg_comparisons(analyses, variables = "edyrs",
                hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
```

`mice` warns "Large sample assumed." here. That is expected: `suest` reports
large-sample statistics, so the pooled degrees of freedom are Rubin's
large-sample values.

`suest_mi()` pools the coefficients and their joint covariance:

```{r mi-pool}
pooled <- suest_mi(analyses)
summary(pooled)
```

`marginaleffects` functions give the same results on `pooled` as on
`analyses`. A list of `suest()` results, one per imputation, or the result
of `with(mitools::imputationList(...), suest(...))` can also be passed to
`suest_mi()`; `marginaleffects` then warns that it could not recover the
original data from a `mids` object, which does not affect `suest()`
results.
